title: Martian Time-Slip
theological_headline: Martian Time-Slip counts among the novels PKD calls politically subversive — inner-space explorations that break through to unfallen hermetic space.
intro:
*Martian Time-Slip* receives a single, glancing mention in the Exegesis, and not for Manfred's autism or the gubble of entropy directly. It appears in a passage where PKD reframes his whole fiction as a political act of expanding "inner space," and names *Martian Time-Slip* among the works that carry that subversive charge. (Lane B: PKD reading his own corpus.)

Because the mention is a bare name in a list, this page does not inflate a developed theology of the schizophrenic-as-seer; it reports the one use PKD actually makes of the title here.
theological_synthesis:
The theological use is political-mystical rather than a reading of the novel's content. In [47:628], borrowing Beethoven's power to "enclose huge volumes of space," PKD argues that his own explorations of inner space are covertly subversive — teaching secret ways to rebel by evasion — and that 2-3-74 was a "total political victory" in which he broke through "into absolute space" of the kind unknown since the Hermetics. This absolute space carries a priori knowledge and power over time such that "time can no longer extinguish the person," which he ties to authentic Christianity.

*Martian Time-Slip* is named — with *Ubik*, *Eye*, and *Stigmata* — as one of the works that is "very subversive" in this sense: fiction that promotes the catalytic metamorphosis PKD says he personally achieved, breaking through to the space where the self is "Adam Kadmon, unfallen and unoccluded." The gloss stays proportionate: the novel is cited as an instrument of that liberation, not analyzed for Manfred or gubble here.

mentions.summary: By using his music to enclose huge volumes of space for the listener Beethoven committed the ultimate political act of liberating—expanding—the individual. Likewise, my space phobia is connected with my own rebelliousness! Unable to deal with _external_ space—i.e., unable to rebel—I have turned to inner space, to exploring it, which, too, is a political act; so my writing, involving inner space, is covertly subversive: it teaches secret ways to rebel (mostly by evasion: escape). This is why the whole psychedelic movement of the 60s was a threat to the authorities; this was the area of the subversive threat I posed—my studies of inner space—in fact—my conceptions of inner space differing from person to person is very radical and politically subversive, I now see, even when it didn't involve drugs. Viewed this way, then, 2-3-74 represents a total political victory by me, in that I broke through _into absolute space_ such as is not even known about following the disappearance of the Hermetics. 2-3-74 can be understood politically if the significance for the nature of the individual in terms of his enclosing space is recognized as basic (e.g., Beethoven's music). This absolute space involves absolute (i.e., a priori) knowledge and power over time in that time can no longer extinguish the person. This relates to authentic Christianity. Hence there really is something very subversive about _Ubik,_ as well as _Eye_ and _Stigmata_ and _Martian Time-Slip._ I personally achieved the catalytic metamorphosis that my writ ing promotes. And my writing may aid others in expanding their inner space— pointing toward what _I_ did: breaking through into absolute (hermetic) space where the self is Adam Kadmon, unfallen and unoccluded! ##

The novel is cited as an instrument of that metamorphosis, not read for Manfred or entropy in this passage.
